reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / Fitzpatrick's Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A chronic disorder of the apocrine sweat glands producing intensely itchy, dome-shaped, skin-coloured to yellowish follicular papules
Characteristically involves apocrine-bearing sites, most commonly the axillae and also the areolae, groin, and pubic area
Predominantly affects women of reproductive age, with pruritus often worse during emotional or thermal sweating
The affected skin may show reduced sweating and sometimes loss or breakage of hair within the involved area
Regarded as an apocrine form of miliaria caused by keratin obstruction of the apocrine duct, leading to duct rupture and inflammation
Symptoms may fluctuate with the menstrual cycle and often improve in pregnancy and after the menopause, implicating hormonal influences
Diagnosis is usually clinical, though biopsy can show the characteristic infundibular and apocrine-duct changes with perifollicular foam cells
Treatment is difficult and includes topical corticosteroids or calcineurin inhibitors, topical retinoids, and measures to reduce sweating, with hormonal and procedural options for resistant disease
reference.pathophysiology: Fox-Fordyce disease is thought to begin with keratotic plugging and obstruction of the apocrine sweat-gland duct at its follicular opening. Retained secretion causes the duct to dilate and eventually rupture, releasing its contents into the surrounding dermis and provoking an intensely itchy inflammatory reaction with characteristic perifollicular foamy (lipid-laden) cells. A hormonal influence is suggested by its predominance in women, its variation with the menstrual cycle, and its tendency to improve during pregnancy and after the menopause, though the precise trigger for the initial ductal plugging remains uncertain.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical diagnosis based on itchy papules confined to apocrine-bearing sites
Skin biopsy in uncertain cases showing infundibular keratin plugging, apocrine-duct change, and perifollicular foam cells
Review of the hormonal and menstrual pattern of symptoms
Assessment of hair changes within the affected areas
redFlags: Secondary infection of excoriated, intensely pruritic lesions
Significant psychosocial impact from chronic itch in exposed and intimate areas
Diagnostic uncertainty requiring biopsy to exclude other follicular disorders
reference.prognosis: Chronic and often persistent, though it tends to improve after the menopause and frequently during pregnancy; treatment controls symptoms with variable success rather than curing the condition.
pitfalls: Mistaking it for simple folliculitis or eccrine miliaria and treating inappropriately
Underestimating the impact of chronic itch and cosmetic concern in intimate sites
Expecting a rapid or complete cure from topical therapy
